text:
A: Hello. Can you hear me alright?
B: Yes, hello, sorry. I wasn't sure if it had started or not.
A: I think it just starts. There's a little timer in the corner, which is slightly ominous.
B: Oh, yes, I see it. Erm, I'm Joanne. Jo. I don't really know what we're meant to talk about, sorry.
A: Alison. I don't think we're meant to talk about anything, I think that's the point. How did you get on with the puzzle?
B: Oh, don't. I was terrible. I got about three and then I just sort of sat there. I don't know if that's what they wanted.
A: I abandoned one halfway, which is what I do with the crossword most mornings, so it felt quite normal.
B: Oh, you do the crossword? The proper one?
A: The cryptic, yes. Badly. My husband says I only do it so I can complain about the setter.
B: I do word searches. They're more my level, if that makes sense. I do them on my break at work.
A: What do you do?
B: I'm a domestic at the hospital. On the wards, cleaning. I've been there eleven years now. I'm on earlies, so I'm up at half five, which is why I look like this, sorry.
A: You look fine. Half five is brutal though. Which hospital?
B: The general in Basingstoke. I've lived there all my life, really. I've never gone more than about five miles, Gary says.
A: There's a lot to be said for that. I'm in Tonbridge. I work for the council, planning, so I spend all day reading about people wanting to put extensions where they shouldn't.
B: Oh, that sounds very clever. I'd worry about getting it wrong.
A: It's mostly reading. And sitting in meetings while people shout at you. You sort of learn not to take it personally. I imagine you get a bit of that too.
B: Not shouting, really. The patients are mostly lovely. The elderly ones especially, they get frightened, you know, and you just have a little chat while you're doing round their bed. Some of them know me by name. Sorry, I'm going on.
A: No, you're not. That's the bit that actually matters, isn't it? The talking.
B: I think so. The nurses haven't always got time, so. Erm, have you got a dog? I saw a lead in your picture.
A: Well spotted. Biscuit. Labrador cross, very elderly and very lazy. He won't go out if it's raining, he just stands in the doorway and looks at me.
B: No! My cat's called Biscuit.
A: Is it really?
B: She's nineteen. She's getting a bit doddery now, she sort of walks into the table leg.
A: That's quite a coincidence. Two elderly Biscuits. Perhaps it's a South East thing.
B: My daughter named her. Kirsty. She was about ten. She's twenty-nine now and she's got a little boy, he's just started saying Nanny Jo.
A: Oh, that's lovely. Mine are thirty-two and twenty-nine, no grandchildren yet. I'm not holding my breath. My daughter's in south London, so I get the train up and we have lunch and she tells me what I'm doing wrong.
B: Kirsty does that. Mostly about my phone.
A: Mine taught me "tbh". I'm not sure I've thanked her for it.
B: My son's in Reading now. Liam. He moved last year for work. I text him more than I should, probably.
A: I don't think there's a should with that. They'd tell you if it was too much. Well, mine would. Bluntly.
B: That's true. I just, I don't know, I miss him, you know. The house is quiet.
A: It is quiet. You get used to it. Sort of. Graham fills it with DIY he never finishes.
B: Gary's the same. There's a shelf in the hall that's been —
A: Since spring?
B: Since Christmas!
A: Oh, you're winning. We've got a timer going, I think we're nearly —
